title: 4,154 orders on a campus trading game

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Picture a trading competition where nobody can lose real money, and still 170 people show up. That's what happened at ÉTS.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Okay, I'm listening. Who ran it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: AlgoÉTS, the student club. Antoine was its president at the time, and the club ran its first campus-wide paper-trading competition on a platform called MarkÉTS.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Paper trading, so fake money, real market behavior.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. And the platform was built and maintained by students. That's the part I like. They weren't renting a tool, they were shipping features while people were actually using it.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Over about four months, the platform executed 4,154 orders. More than 170 participants took part, and the leaderboards had returns near sixty percent.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Sixty percent? On play money, sure, but that's still a fun leaderboard to chase.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It is. And there's an engineering number too. Platform uptime stayed above ninety-nine percent, and the team shipped more than fifteen features during the live competition.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Shipping features mid-contest. That sounds stressful.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Probably! The club also brought in six new developers and grew to twenty members. Partners included ÉTS and FÉRIQUE.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The club's own summary names three things: more platform work, machine learning and AI strategies, and more contests.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the takeaway is that a student club can run something that behaves like a real product.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. The figures come from the club summary Antoine featured on his LinkedIn, and the written post has the details and the source.
